input: Learn to read music notation from scratch

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Music notation covers a huge range — basic note names and values, clefs, key signatures, time signatures, dynamics, articulation, chord notation, etc. Knowing how far they want to go shapes the entire curriculum depth.
Whether this is for a child or an adult changes the learning approach, materials, and pacing significantly.

The instrument they play (or plan to play) determines which clef(s) to prioritise — e.g. treble for guitar/violin, bass for bass guitar, grand staff for piano — making the learning highly instrument-specific.
How much time per day or week they can dedicate directly affects how the plan is broken into sessions and how long reaching fluency will realistically take.
Some people learn best through apps, others through printed workbooks, video lessons, or a human teacher. The preferred learning medium shapes what resources to recommend.
Their definition of 'done' could range from recognising note names on a staff to sight-reading a simple piece in real time — knowing this sets a concrete target for the plan.
Whether they want a structured daily routine, a checklist of milestones, or a curated resource list determines the immediate next action and the format of the plan.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to read music notation from scratch
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to build music reading skills starting with no prior knowledge of standard notation.

questions.title: Which clef or instrument is this notation for?
questions.description: Knowing the target instrument tells us which clef(s) to focus on first — treble, bass, alto, or grand staff — so the learning path is immediately practical rather than generic.

questions.title: How far into notation do you want to go?
questions.description: Clarifies the depth of scope — from basic note names and rhythms only, up through key signatures, time signatures, dynamics, articulation marks, and beyond.

questions.title: What is your concrete end goal with reading music?
questions.description: Defines success criteria — e.g. recognise note names on a page, play through a simple printed piece, or sight-read fluently in real time.

questions.title: How much time can you study each day or week?
questions.description: Time availability is the primary constraint that determines session length, milestone spacing, and a realistic timeline to reach the goal.

questions.title: Who is learning — you, a child, or someone else?
questions.description: The learner's age and background changes recommended materials, teaching style, and the complexity of explanations in the plan.

questions.title: Do you prefer apps, books, videos, or a live teacher?
questions.description: Learning medium preference shapes which specific resources and tools get recommended — interactive apps like Simply Piano, printed workbooks, YouTube channels, or one-on-one lessons.

questions.title: What format do you want the plan delivered in?
questions.description: Determines the logistics and immediate next action — a structured daily schedule, a checklist of topics/milestones, a curated reading list, or a step-by-step roadmap document.
